newsitem.title: EGYPT: Rebels say they advance, Sudan declares holy war.
newsitem.headline: Rebels say they advance, Sudan declares holy war.

text.p: An alliance of Sudanese rebels said their forces were advancing on Wednesday on the southern Blue Nile city of Damazin where a hydro-electric station supplies the Sudanese capital Khartoum with most of its power.
Yassir Arman, spokesman of the Southern Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), told Reuters in Eritrea that the rebels were within 80 km (50 miles) of Damazin and advancing.
Damazin is about 480 km (300 miles) southeast of Khartoum and supplies Khartoum with up to 80 percent of its power.
The rebels say their objective is not to capture the capital but to strangle it and provoke an uprising against the Islamist military government of President Omar Hassan al-Bashir.
Arman said the latest rebel advance, which has seen two border towns and several garrisons captured since Sunday, was a turning point in the 13-year war against Khartoum.

"This operation is to enable the mass movement inside Sudan to wage an uprising against the military junta there. By advancing on Damazin we are piling economic and military pressure on the junta," Arman said.

The SPLA, the largest group of rebels in the mostly Christian and animist south, has joined forces with the National Democratic Alliance (NDA), an umbrella group whose military forces are mainly northerners based in Eritrea.
The rebels said this week's offensive was their first combined operation and that it had rattled Khartoum.
Lieutenant-General Bashir, who seized power in a 1989 coup, said on Tuesday that government troops heading to the front were embarking on a jihad or holy war.

"Scores of mujahidin (jihad fighters) are now hurrying towards the theatre of operation in order to defend the eastern front and teach the aggressors and the traitors a lesson they will never forget," Sudanese radio quoted Bashir as saying in a report monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation.
"Bashir said political and diplomatic channels (to Ethiopia) had been closed. He said the only thing left now was the power of the gun," the radio added.
Ethiopia says it has nothing to do with the attacks on Sudanese garrisons in Blue Nile province southeast of Khartoum.

The SPLA also said the rebel alliance had made advances far to the northeast of Damazin, near the town of Kassala which is close to the Eritrean border and lies about 450 km (280 miles) east of Khartoum.
The Sudanese have referred only obliquely to the rebel role in the fighting. Bashir called them Ethiopia's agents.
"Its agents", he said, "have nakedly violated Sudan's territorial integrity and provoked Moslems, with no respect for the holy month of Ramadan."
The fasting month began in most Islamic countries last Friday. Moslems may not eat or drink from dawn to dusk but those fighting a jihad are excused fasting.
Residents of Khartoum said some members of the public had responded to the government's call for general mobilisation against the rebels.

They have been enlisting in the People's Defence Forces, a paramilitary organisation set up after Bashir's coup to help the army fight the rebels in the south. Khartoum University closed on Tuesday so that students could go to the front and fight.
Bashir's government has been dominated by members of the National Islamic Front, the Islamist movement led by speaker of parliament Hassan al-Turabi.
It has antagonised most of Sudan's neighbours with its support for other Islamist movements seeking to overthrow their own governments.
Ethiopia has grown increasingly hostile, especially after it accused the Sudanese of helping the Egyptian Islamists who tried to kill Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Addis Ababa in 1995.
